title: Bengaluru-Born Astronomer Ramya Anche to Lead NASA's $20 Million PUFFINS Mission
excerpt: Ramya Anche of the University of Arizona will lead PUFFINS, a $20 million NASA Pioneers mission using a 10-inch ultraviolet telescope to decode interstellar dust from about 70 stars ahead of a 2030 launch.
body:
• NASA has awarded $20 million to a University of Arizona team to build PUFFINS, a small space telescope that will study interstellar dust by measuring polarized ultraviolet light from about 70 stars.
  • The mission is led by Ramya Anche, an assistant research professor at Steward Observatory who developed the winning proposal while still a postdoctoral researcher.
  • PUFFINS will use a 10-inch telescope in low-Earth orbit and a technique, ultraviolet spectropolarimetry, that has not flown in space in nearly three decades.
  • The mission is in early design, targets launch in 2030, and is meant to help define a future instrument for NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory.

NASA has awarded $20 million to a University of Arizona team building a small space telescope to study the dust between stars, and the mission will be led by Bengaluru-born astronomer Ramya Anche, according to the university and India Today reporting on the selection.

Anche, an assistant research professor at the university's Steward Observatory, is principal investigator of PUFFINS — Polarimetry in the Ultraviolet to Find Features in INterStellar dust. From low-Earth orbit, its 10-inch telescope, roughly the size of a dinner plate, will observe about 70 stars and measure how their ultraviolet light has been changed by dust on the way to Earth.

"PUFFINS will change how we understand the dust between stars."

— Ramya Anche, Principal Investigator, PUFFINS

Why dust, and why polarization

Interstellar dust makes up only about 1% of the visible mass of the Milky Way, yet it affects almost every part of astrophysics, according to the University of Arizona. Dust helps shield complex molecules, cools the clouds where stars form, and eventually becomes part of new stars and planets. Its smallest grains, smaller than about 50 nanometers, are largely invisible to optical and infrared telescopes.

PUFFINS approaches the problem through polarization, the orientation of light. Tiny silicate grains spin and align with the galaxy's magnetic field, acting as a filter that polarizes starlight passing through them. Measuring that polarization across ultraviolet wavelengths can reveal what the smallest grains are made of, how they form, and how they behave in extreme environments. The mission site describes the same three aims: probing small-grain alignment below 3200 angstroms, determining the origin of polarization in the 2175-angstrom extinction feature, and surveying ultraviolet polarization across varied lines of sight.

A first in nearly 30 years

The university says PUFFINS will use spectropolarimetry in space for the first time in nearly three decades. Science principal investigator B-G Andersson of McDonald Observatory at the University of Texas at Austin has studied dust-grain alignment for more than 20 years. The team says the mission addresses a question that has stood since interstellar polarization was discovered in 1949.

https://x.com/NASA/status/2110823965954637903

Anche said the project is the culmination of more than a decade of instrument-building work in polarimetry and will be the first instrument she helped design to be built and launched. Steward Observatory director Buell Jannuzi noted she led the winning NASA proposal while still a postdoctoral researcher, which he described as uncommon support for an early-career scientist.

Part of a larger Arizona run

PUFFINS is the second mission led by the University of Arizona under NASA's Astrophysics Pioneers program, launched in 2020 to fund compelling science on small platforms led by early- and mid-career researchers. The university also leads Aspera, expected to launch early next year, and runs operations for Pandora, launched in January. PUFFINS partners include McDonald Observatory and an international network of scientists, with corporate partners Ascending Node Technologies in Tucson and SFL Missions Inc. in Toronto.

Kyle Van Gorkom, an early-career Steward faculty member, is deputy principal investigator and leads spacecraft interface work. The university says graduate and undergraduate researchers are embedded in instrument development, making the mission a training ground as well as a science program.

What happens next

PUFFINS is in early design. Its own timeline lists a systems requirements review in 2027, a critical design review in 2028, and launch in 2030. While the payload is built, the science team will collect visible and infrared spectropolarimetry of target stars from ground telescopes to complement the space data.

The longer payoff is NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory, the flagship telescope planned for the 2040s. It may carry an ultraviolet spectropolarimeter, and PUFFINS data can help define what that instrument should do. For Indian and Indian American students in astronomy, Anche's path — from Bengaluru to leading a NASA mission as an early-career researcher — is also a concrete example that the Pioneers program was designed to create: a first mission leadership role without waiting for a flagship-scale career.
